scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Architecture of a Flower
This is Alarippu. 19th century.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Alarippu was formalized by the Tanjore Quartet, four brothers (Chinnayya, Ponniah, Sivanandam, and Vadivelu) who were prominent musicians and dance scholars in the 19th-century Tanjore court.
They structured the dance into five different talas (rhythmic cycles) to provide a systematic introduction to Bharatanatyam technique.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: As an invocation, it is performed at the very beginning of a Bharatanatyam recital.
It symbolizes the 'blossoming' of the dancer's body and mind, serving as a prayer and a physical warm-up to prepare for the spiritual journey of the dance.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance starts with the feet together (Samapada) and progresses through various levels of height, including the signature Araimandi posture.
It focuses on the coordination of the neck, eyes, and head.
The movement begins with subtle isolations and builds into larger rhythmic patterns involving the arms and legs, following the beat of the mridangam.
Watch for Griva Bheda, Araimandi.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is primarily rhythmic, featuring a verbal percussionist (Nattuvanar) who recites rhythmic syllables and a mridangist who plays the mridangam drum.
The piece is defined by its Tala (rhythmic cycle) rather than a melodic raga, though a simple drone or melodic accompaniment may be present.
Listen for the Mridangam, Cymbals (Manjira), Nattuvanar's voice.
The pulse is Variable (3, 4, 5, 7, or 9 beats depending on the Jathi).

The sound is dominated by the sharp, resonant strikes of the mridangam and the crisp, percussive vocalizations of the Nattuvanar. There is no melodic singing, creating a focused, rhythmic atmosphere that highlights the dancer's footwork.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers typically wear the traditional Bharatanatyam sari or dress with a pleated front that fans out during the Araimandi posture.
The setting is usually a formal stage or a temple courtyard, where the dancer performs facing the audience and the deity.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The Tanjore Quartet (Chinnayya, Ponniah, Sivanandam, and Vadivelu) are the central figures responsible for creating the five talas of Alarippu.

While the core structure remains consistent within Bharatanatyam, the piece can be performed in five different Jathis (Tisra, Chatusra, Khanda, Misra, and Sankeerna), which alter the rhythmic complexity.
Alarippu is the first step in the Margam, the traditional sequence of Bharatanatyam pieces, followed by Jatiswaram, Shabdam, and Varnam.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Alarippu is parent of Bharatanatyam: Alarippu is the foundational opening piece of the Bharatanatyam repertoire.
Alarippu is sibling of Jatiswaram: The second piece in the Margam, which adds melody to the pure rhythm of Alarippu.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Alarippu is a ritual offering to the gods and the guru; it should be performed with a sense of devotion and respect. Outsiders should observe quietly and avoid interrupting the dancer's initial salutations.
